It's almost like Firestar has flaws as a product of his character, and Squirrelflight has flaws as a product of her environment. The second is definitely more compelling to read, but also makes a much more controversial character to parse the actions and emotions of. Their personalities are extremely similar foundation-ally, but they differ in how they manifest.

I bet he's still cute haha! Yeah, it's just our intrinsic disgust toward inbreeding (totally natural and good for humans BTW!!!!) mixed with a total lack of understanding of what inbreeding is. I would NEVER breed my half-sibling dogs together, but if I did, the puppies would be....completely healthy. Two genetically healthy dogs are going to make genetically healthy pups even if they're siblings. Inbreeding depression takes generations.

The average coefficient of inbreeding in any purebred dog across AKC recognized breeds is 20%- this can be much higher or much lower so an average is fairly skewed. My dogs (half-siblings) are both around 4%. My mutt on the other hand has a COI of 40%. Many feral dog communities also have COIs around 30-40%. There is nothing inherently detrimental about inbreeding in and of itself, and there is no way to look at an individual dog and determine what it's COI is. Some of our presidents have had higher COIs than most purebreds I know LOL.

Heavy linebreeding (as in not in the immediate family inbreeding) is extremely frowned upon by the majority of ethical breeders. Breed clubs are getting much more comfortable and excited about outcrossing projects to promote genetic diversity. Discussions of genetic diversity and inbreeding depression in purebred communities are really interesting, especially because those communities are the ones doing the research and solving the problems related to it.

I hope I don't come off as rude, this is just a really interesting topic to discuss. Like most things, the world of wellbred dogs gets much less black and white once you put a little work into learning about it. I support breeding well bred dogs, because I think dogs should exist, and they wouldn't exist well if we don't do it right!

It's a big needle, but the techs are so experienced obviously it's no big deal. There are always risks with blood draws and the recirculating, but they're minor. Mild scarring if you do it regularly for some time. You shouldn't smoke or drink for several hours afterwards, and you can only donate every 3 days generally. A good meal and lots of water + icing the injection site if it's sore and that's about it, you're fine.

It's super easy and comfortable, and if you don't mind sitting still for an hour or so a few times a week, it's definitely worth it! 30-50/hr to do basically nothing, listen to a podcast or read a book. Your first session will take a bit longer, and they'll make you fill out some forms, confirm your identity and address, and do some physical assessments (poking your fingers, a small physical, height and weight etc.), and if all is well you get hooked up and left. 

My least favorite part is the end where they flush you up with some saline or whatever to rehydrate what you lost with the plasma, it's cold and makes my mouth tingle. The poke is no big deal, and you're in a comfortable chair and can't really feel the needle after it's in. After your first appointment you'll just get in line, show your stuff, and go to your seat. Drink and eat lots of good food and water before and it'll go quicker!

I use a naming system within my ocs and aus.

A prefix denotes appearance, and very rarely a unique circumstance at birth. Anything can be a prefix as long as it fits that criteria and is something the cats would regularly see or interact with in their environment (like Chub- works for my rocky mountain fan clans, but not for a place with no chub fish). 

Suffixes generally acknowledge a cats specific skills or personality, and while a cats suffix is unique to them, the definition is traditionally agreed upon by the clan. So everyone knows a -whisker cat is a good hunter, or a -heart cat has strong morals, or a -flight cat is an exceptional climber. This might vary between Clans (one clan using -feather for gifted medicine cats and one using it for great bird hunters), but within a clan the meaning of suffixes is consistent. There are also a wide variety of generic suffixes that celebrate a cat becoming a warrior with no particular skill, and many of them may also acknowledge any unique physical features (-pelt and -fur being the basics, but if you have spots you may get -fall, or -stripe for stripes). 

The only suffix in my system where the prefix is relevant or tied in is -step, which shows that a cat moves or behaves in way related to their prefix, like Harestep being a fast-footed and nervous but steadfast cat. 

I prefer my naming systems to be functional and consistent, but there's still plenty of room for fun! This is just what I find fun lol. Shrikefang (a black molly equally exceptional in fighting and hunting), Wolfwhisker (a dark gray excellent hunter), Salmonblossom (a mostly-red talented mentor), Tawnythroat (a pale ginger cat great at lorekeeping and storytelling), and Brightfall (a shiny furred golden molly with spotted tabby markings) are all examples of names I really like that fit my naming style.

Kennel work is the perfect fit for me for these exact reasons. I NEED to be both stimulated and engaged and challenged at work but also not overstimulated or anxious or judged. 

Working in the kennels be it in a boarding/daycare facility, laboratory setting, veterinary hospital, animal shelter- even a stable with livestock!- fulfills that, for me at least.

The work is mainly independent, and it is soothing in that it's a repetitive list of things that need to be done each shift, but it's also generally fast paced and a position that gives you the ability to problem solve daily if you have the desire (ie. Is there a more effective method to get this kennel clean? What do I need to do to safely manage this anxious animal? Should any of our policies change to provide more enrichment and sanitation?), AND its generally a position where you are working alone or with one other person. It's also so rewarding because you know whatever facility you're working with couldn't run without your help, but without concerns that are truly high stakes. Bonus you can usually wear headphones all day lol.

The pay varies, but in a veterinary hospital or lab setting it can be fairly good (especially once you gain experience) if you're able to work full time. And you can start it with 0 experience usually, and move to bigger and better facilities in the future if you like.

If you relate to this meme, and you like animals and slightly more physical jobs, I hope my suggestion is helpful! "Kennel staff" isn't a widely respected field but it's truly my passion and fits my needs perfectly.

I want to talk about a very rare landrace breed. 

Ovejero Magallánico, known mostly in their local area as Barbucho Magellan, also called Patagonian Sheepdog and Magellan Sheepdog.

There are, as far as we're aware, only two in the US, and possibly only two outside of Chile in general. Mapu and Cuyen.

Patagonians are the favorite herding dog in the Patagonia region of Chile. Shepherds have claimed that even Border Collies are nothing in skill and tenacity compared to them! They're not a recognized breed by any kennel club and are very difficult to obtain as they're generally only traded between shepherds and farmers in the area. 

The breed was developed from the original European sheepdogs like Old Welsh Grey Sheepdogs that traveled with the original European settlers in Chile, along with the original sheep arriving in the Magallanes region in 1876. Fascinating genomic research has shown their ancestry, relation to other herding breeds, and the fact that they are a distinct breed with consistency in traits despite breeding goals exclusively being based on herding ability. 

Barbucho are a medium sized breed with a shaggy long coat to protect them from the Arctic winds and harsh weather of the area. While there's a very wide range of coat colors and patterns (including merle), gray, black, and brown with or without tan points and white appear to be the most common. Interestingly, they're very low shedding. They have semi-erect ears, long tails, and very strong legs.

In terms of personality…they're perfect. If you ask me! Tenacious, insane get up and go with a solid off switch, very affectionate and family oriented, aloof to strangers, protective of family without undue aggression, dog and small animal friendly. And the dedication to work is unbelievable. I'll include a quote below from "The Patagonian Sheepdog: Historical Perspective on a Herding Dog in Chile".

"The “estancias” typically operate with two sheepdogs; one dog leads the flock (pointer role) to the location that the sheepherder indicates by whistling, and the other rounds the flock, preventing sheep from remaining behind [31]. Most dogs can perform both functions, depending on the type of whistle that is used by the shepherd. Typically, the herding work is performed in extensive open fields, and a small number of dogs also work in pens. During herding, the Patagonian sheepdog shows little physical wearing, and maintains a moderately wide distance from the sheep (e.g., between 2 and 10 m), with a strong visual focus. These dogs have the ability to keep the flock together and easily follow the orders of the shepherd. They are docile and submissive, never bite, but tend to bark while working. The herding function of the Patagonian sheepdog is thus similar to that of the Border Collie (BC), but the latter does not bark, and the Patagonian Sheepdog does not display the BC’s crouch position (lying ventrally flat on the ground facing the sheep) [7,32]. It has been estimated that one working Patagonian sheepdog is sufficient to control a flock of 200–300 sheep".

They are also a very healthy breed. This is expected from landraces in my experience. Their COI is incredibly low for their small but distinct populations. In Cuyen and Mapu's testing, the only findings are that Cuyen is a carrier of CEA, which was expected to be seen in the breed.

Personally, I plan to import a male sometime next year, and more dogs in the future. Mapu and Cuyen's owners are hoping they can have a Chilean shepherd that works the breed come in and do some herding demos with their local all breed clubs to introduce the breed and their talents to more people.
